passage:
Tuesday, 11 pm
Shankar did it again at dinner. Someone mentioned a new restaurant and he said, "Madhav wouldn't know, he's never eaten with a fork," and the table laughed. I laughed too. I always laugh.
Now I'm lying here doing the maths. If I say something tomorrow, will it become a big scene? Will they say I can't take a joke? Maybe I am oversensitive. It was one line. But it's also the fourth line this month, and I've noticed I've stopped ordering anything unfamiliar when we go out, just in case.
Option 1: say it privately to Shankar. Option 2: let it go and save my energy for exams.
Both seem fine. Neither feels light. What's tiring is carrying it around all night like this, deciding.
Maybe I'll talk to Shankar after the morning lab.

qa.q: What did Shankar say about Madhav at dinner?
qa.a: He said Madhav wouldn't know, he's never eaten with a fork.

qa.q: What worries Madhav about speaking up tomorrow?
qa.a: He worries it will become a big scene, that they'll say he can't take a joke, and that maybe he is oversensitive.

qa.q: Madhav is leaning towards talking to Shankar after the morning lab. Why is that a reasonable choice, alongside letting it go?
qa.a: A private word could stop the pattern without a scene; letting it go is also valid, but a sleepless night shows that silence has a cost too.

qa.q: How might Shankar react if Madhav raises it privately?
qa.a: Shankar might be defensive at first, but he may not realise his jokes have piled up, and hearing about the fourth line might surprise him.

grounding: A young adult hears a demeaning joke about his background and weighs whether speaking up is worth the friction, tired from carrying it.

Nikita: ok I need a sanity check
Nikita: in the team meeting, Siddhesh said "girls can do the slides, boys will handle the coding"
Nikita: I literally wrote half the code last sprint
Tanuja: WHAT

Nikita: if I bring it up I'm difficult. if I don't, I'm on slides forever
Tanuja: what if you just message him: "I'd like to stay on the backend, I built the login module"
Nikita: that's... actually doable. no speech needed

Nikita: I'm so tired of doing this maths in my head
Tanuja: I know. I'm here either way

qa.q: What did Siddhesh say in the team meeting?
qa.a: "Girls can do the slides, boys will handle the coding."

qa.q: What is Nikita worried about on each side of the choice?
qa.a: If Nikita speaks up, being seen as difficult; if not, being stuck on slides forever.

qa.q: Why is Tanuja's suggested message a useful option?
qa.a: It asks for the work Nikita wants, backed by the login module, without a big confrontation, while still leaving silence as a valid choice.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel reading these messages?
qa.a: Tanuja seems angry on Nikita's behalf, given the "WHAT", but careful not to push, wanting Nikita to feel supported either way.

grounding: A young adult hears a demeaning remark in a meeting, wonders if they are overreacting, and weighs speaking up against the friction it may cause.

passage: The bus to the district college was late again, and the tea-stall owner at the kasba stand had an opinion, as always. "Two years of college, and then? Rotis are rotis, beti, degree or no degree." The men on the bench chuckled. Zeenat's hand tightened on her file. Dilnaz glanced at her, waiting. Zeenat could say it: that she had topped the first-year accounts exam, that her rotis were none of his business. But the bus was coming, he gave her father credit in bad months, and she'd have to stand here every morning. Was it even worth it? Maybe she was being too touchy. She said nothing and climbed on. At the window, Dilnaz squeezed her hand. "You can say it tomorrow. Or never. Both are fine." Zeenat nodded, but the sentence sat in her chest all the way to college.

qa.q: Which exam had Zeenat topped?
qa.a: She had topped the first-year accounts exam.

qa.q: What made Zeenat hesitate to answer the tea-stall owner?
qa.a: She worried about the cost: he gave her father credit in bad months, she'd face him every morning, and she wondered if she was too touchy.

qa.q: Dilnaz says "You can say it tomorrow. Or never." Why is that a helpful way to support Zeenat?
qa.a: It leaves the decision with Zeenat and treats both speaking and staying quiet as legitimate, instead of adding pressure.

qa.q: How might the tea-stall owner see his own remark?
qa.a: He probably thinks it was harmless teasing, not realising how it sits with Zeenat all the way to college.

grounding: A young woman hears a belittling remark about her studies and weighs the cost of answering, choosing silence this time but carrying it with her.

passage: On the third day of his placement on a hospital ward in Leeds, Gabriel was changing a dressing when Nadia, his mentor, breezed past and told the patient, "Don't mind him, he's our male nurse. Couldn't get into medicine, bless him." The patient chuckled. Gabriel kept his hands steady. It wasn't true; nursing had been his first choice since he'd sat by his grandfather's bed at fourteen. On the bus home he turned it over and over. Was he being touchy? She'd said it with a smile. If he raised it, she'd be signing off his competencies next week. If he didn't, he'd hear it again, and again he'd smile. He typed her a message, deleted it, typed a shorter one. His thumb hovered. Then he slid the phone into his pocket, too tired to decide tonight, and rested his forehead against the cold window.

qa.q: What did Nadia tell the patient about Gabriel?
qa.a: "Don't mind him, he's our male nurse. Couldn't get into medicine, bless him."

qa.q: What was Gabriel worried about as he weighed whether to speak up?
qa.a: He wondered if he was being touchy, and he worried that raising it with his mentor could cost him, since she would be signing off his competencies next week.

qa.q: With his thumb over the message, what choices did Gabriel have, and what would each cost?
qa.a: He could send a short, calm message or ask for a quiet word, risking friction; or let it go for now, which avoids conflict but may mean carrying the same remark again. Either is a fair choice.

qa.q: How might Nadia see things if Gabriel never mentions it?
qa.a: Nadia would likely think it was harmless teasing and keep repeating it, never knowing it followed Gabriel all the way home on the bus.

grounding: A nursing student hears a demeaning remark from his mentor and weighs whether speaking up is worth the friction, while silence is already wearing on him.

passage: The placement cell smelt of toner and old files. Hansa handed over her form for the core mechanical drive, and the officer, not unkindly, slid a second sheet across. "Take the HR one also, beta. Girls finally settle there, no? Less pressure." Behind her, Lalremsiami stopped scrolling. Hansa felt heat climb her neck. Four years of lathe work, a gold in the design project. Was she overreacting to one tired man's habit? He signed the shortlists, and twenty people were in the queue. Staying quiet would be easy; she'd been doing it since first year, and it was getting heavy. She pushed the HR sheet back, gently. "Only mechanical, sir. That's the job I want." He shrugged and stamped her form. Outside, her hands were shaking. Lalremsiami bumped her shoulder. "Okay?" "Ask me tomorrow," Hansa said, and laughed, a little.

qa.q: What did the officer slide across to Hansa?
qa.a: A second sheet, the HR form.

qa.q: Why did Hansa hesitate before answering the officer?
qa.a: She wondered whether she was overreacting to one tired man's habit, and she knew he signed the shortlists, so speaking up might cost her.

qa.q: What choice did Hansa make at the turning point, and why did it suit the moment?
qa.a: She pushed the HR sheet back and calmly said she only wanted mechanical, a short, clear reply that stated what she wanted without starting a fight in front of the queue.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have experienced watching the exchange?
qa.a: Lalremsiami noticed at once and stopped scrolling; the shoulder bump afterwards shows they understood the small reply had cost Hansa something.

grounding: A final-year student hears a demeaning remark about girls from the placement officer, weighs the cost of answering, and chooses a brief, calm reply, having grown tired of silence.
